**R2 Nord Details:**

- **No reservation needed** - Buy at station machines (accepts cards)
- **No app required**
- **How it works:** If at T1, take free shuttle to T2. Train station is at T2. Take R2 Nord direction "Maçanet-Massanes" or "Barcelona"
- **Frequency:** Every 30 minutes

**Step 2: Barcelona Sants to Valencia (High-Speed AVE or Euromed)**

|------------|----------|------|-------|
| **AVE** | 2h 40min | €35-60/person | Fastest, most comfortable |

### How to Book in Renfe App (Step-by-Step)

1. Open **Renfe app**
2. Tap **"Buy tickets"**
3. **DEPARTURE station:** Type "Barcelona" and select **BARCELONA-SANTS**
4. **ARRIVAL station:** Type "Valencia" and select **VALENCIA-JOAQUÍN SOROLLA**

8. **Train:** Select **Euromed** for scenic coastal views (3h) or AVE for faster (2h 40min)
9. **Fare type:** "Elige" for flexibility (in case flight is delayed)
10. **Seat selection:** Pick **window seats on RIGHT side** for Mediterranean views

**Best Seats for Scenic Views:**
- This is one of Spain's MOST SCENIC train routes!
- **RIGHT side window seats** = Mediterranean coast, beaches, orange groves
- **Euromed** runs closer to coast than AVE = better views (worth extra 20 min!)

- Strollers fit in luggage areas on trains
- Changing facilities available on AVE trains

- Bring supplies for ~4-hour journey

## Valencia: What to Do (May 27-28)

### Recommendations

**1. Casa Carmela Paella Lunch** ⭐ BOOKED

- **What:** Traditional wood-fired paella at a legendary local restaurant (since 1922)
- **Why:** This is how paella is SUPPOSED to be made - wood fire, no gas, no shortcuts. Locals eat here.
- **When:** **Thursday May 28, 2026 at 1:00 PM Spain time** (day after arrival)
- **Cost:** €20-30/person
- **Distance:** 10-15 min walk from your beach house (it's on your street!)
- **Address:** Carrer d'Isabel de Villena, 155
- **Order:** Paella Valenciana (chicken, rabbit, beans) for traditional, or Paella de Mariscos (seafood)
- **Tip:** They cook to order, so expect 20-30 min wait - worth it!

**2. Mercado Central (Central Market)**

- **What:** One of Europe's largest and most beautiful food markets (1,000+ stalls)
- **Why:** Stunning 1914 Art Nouveau building, authentic local food experience
- **Cost:** Free entry; budget €10-20/person for tastings and snacks
- **Distance:** 20 min taxi from accommodation (~€12-15)
- **When:** Open Mon-Sat 7:30 AM - 3:00 PM (closed Sundays)
- **Booking:** None needed
- **Note:** May 28 is a flexible day - could visit then or May 27 afternoon if you have energy after travel

**3. City of Arts and Sciences**

- **What:** Stunning futuristic architecture complex with aquarium, science museum, IMAX
- **Why:** Incredible architecture by Santiago Calatrava, great for kids
- **Cost:**
  - L'Oceanogràfic (aquarium): €35-40/person, kids discounted
  - Science Museum: €8-10/person
  - Combined tickets available: €30-35/person
- **Distance:** 15 min taxi from accommodation (~€10)
- **Duration:** Half day to full day
- **Booking:** Can book online at [cac.es](https://www.cac.es/en/) or same-day at ticket office
- **Tip:** The aquarium (L'Oceanogràfic) is Europe's largest - great for Elise!

**4. Turia Gardens Walk/Run**

- **What:** 9km park in a former riverbed running through the city
- **Why:** Perfect for morning jog or family walk, playgrounds for kids
- **Cost:** Free
- **Distance:** Accessible from City of Arts and Sciences
- **Booking:** None needed

**5. Old Town Walking**

- **What:** Historic Valencia - cathedral, Plaza de la Virgen, La Lonja (UNESCO Silk Exchange)
- **Why:** Beautiful architecture, authentic atmosphere
- **Cost:** Free to walk; La Lonja entry ~€2; Cathedral tower climb ~€8
- **Distance:** 20 min taxi from accommodation
- **Booking:** None needed
- **Tip:** La Lonja de la Seda (Silk Exchange) is a stunning 15th-century Gothic building - quick visit, very impressive

**6. Beach Time**

- **What:** Malvarrosa Beach - wide sandy beach with promenade
- **Why:** You're 3-5 min walk from it! Relax, swim, walk
- **Cost:** Free
- **Water temp:** ~20°C (68°F) in late May - refreshing but swimmable
- **Tip:** Beach promenade has restaurants for lunch/dinner with sea views

**For Teenagers (Carson & Harrison):**

- City of Arts and Sciences - futuristic architecture, science museum
- Beach + swimming
- Old town exploration

**For Elise:**

- Aquarium (L'Oceanogràfic) - dolphins, sharks, penguins
- Beach + pool at house
- Turia Gardens playgrounds

**For Valerie:**

- Mercado Central (walking, sitting areas)
- Beach walks on flat promenade
- Old town at relaxed pace

| **Mercado de San Miguel** | Gourmet grazing - olives, jamón, croquettes | €15-25 | No - just wander |
| **DiverXO** | 3 Michelin stars, wild experience | €250+ | YES - months ahead (if you want to splurge BIG) |

**Madrid's Secret Weapon - Vermut Culture:**

Madrid does Sunday "vermut" (vermouth hour) like nowhere else. Find any old bar around noon, order a vermut (vermouth on tap with an olive), and some simple tapas. It's how locals spend Sunday. June 1 is a Monday, but vermut culture is enjoyable any day - the tradition just peaks on Sundays.

**Must-Try Foods in Madrid:**

- **Churros con chocolate** - At San Ginés! Dip thick churros in drinking chocolate
- **Cocido madrileño** - Hearty chickpea stew with meats (served in courses - ask for "completo")
- **Bocadillo de calamares** - Fried squid rings on bread. Sounds weird. Trust me. Get it near Plaza Mayor.
- **Oreja** - Pig ear (for the adventurous!)
- **Callos** - Tripe stew (another adventurous one - very traditional)
- **Jamón ibérico** - The good stuff. Ask for "bellota" (acorn-fed) at any bar.

# Pre-Travel Checklist

## Documents

- Collect passport numbers for all 9 travelers
- Verify passports valid through December 2026
- **Visa:** NOT REQUIRED for US citizens (under 90 days)
- Photo/copy all passports (store separately)
- Save flight confirmations to phones

## Health

- Any needed medications (plus extras)
- Travel insurance
- Check no vaccine requirements

## Packing

Spain in late May / early June: **18–29°C (65–85°F)** per Joe's wedding-weekend forecast — warm, sunny, dry. Wedding night: ~25°C (77°F) at ceremony, ~21°C (70°F) by midnight. You'll walk **a lot** on cobblestones — prioritize comfort over fashion except wedding Sunday.

### Everyone

| Item | Notes |
| ---- | ----- |
| **Power adapters** | **EU Type C** (230V). Bring 2–3 if sharing rooms. |
| **Portable batteries** | Full days of maps, photos, tickets. |
| **Comfortable walking shoes** | Broken-in sneakers or walking sandals. Cobblestones + 15k steps/day. |
| **Light layers** | Morning/evening can be cool (~16°C). Cardigan or light jacket. |
| **Sun protection** | Hat, sunglasses, sunscreen — Mediterranean UV is real. |
| **Day bag / crossbody** | Small pack for water, snacks, tickets, light jacket. |
| **Medications** | Bring extras + keep in carry-on. |
| **Copies of passports** | Photo on phone + paper copy stored separately. |

### Wedding Weekend (May 29–31)

| Who | What to pack / plan |
| --- | ------------------- |
| **Chandler (groomsmen party)** | Rent tux in Barcelona (Casa Gay). Bring **black dress shoes** (any black leather — not patent required). White shirt if rental doesn't include one. |
| **Angela, Valerie, Elise** | **Black dress or black formal outfit** for Sunday wedding. Comfortable dress shoes for cobblestones — consider block heel or elegant flats. |
| **Annalise (sister)** | **Black dress or gown** — tux not required. Same shoe advice. Optional: own hair/makeup tools if skipping pro styling. |
| **Brandon** | Match men's guidance if attending wedding events — black tux or dark formal suit if not in wedding party. |
| **Carson, Harrison (teens)** | Smart casual for events; dark formal for Sunday if requested. Comfortable shoes for tour day (May 30 is long). |
| **All adults** | May 30: smart casual for La Pedrera / Sagrada / tapas tour. May 29 welcome party: smart casual. May 31: black formal. |

### Traveling with Harlan (baby, ~1 year)

| Item | Notes |
| ---- | ----- |
| **Stroller** | Lightweight umbrella stroller strongly recommended — Barcelona Gothic Quarter has steps and narrow alleys; Madrid/Valencia flatter but lots of walking. |
| **Baby carrier** | Backup for stairs and crowded metro. |
| **Diapers / wipes** | Pack 2–3 days in carry-on; buy rest in Spain (DIA, Mercadona, Carrefour). |
| **Formula / snacks** | Bring familiar brands if picky; Spain has equivalents but names differ. |
| **Light blanket / sun shade** | Stroller shade or hat for beach days in Valencia. |
| **Sleep** | **Crib confirmed** Valencia (Maria Pilar) and Madrid (Elena). Pack familiar sleep sack / lovey. |
| **Pace** | Plan slower mornings; Harlan doesn't need wedding formal wear — comfortable cute outfit for photos is fine. |

### Clothes by City (casual days)

| City | Day vibe | Pack |
| ---- | -------- | ---- |
| **Valencia** | Beach / pool | Swimsuits, cover-ups, sandals, one nicer outfit for paella lunch |
| **Barcelona** | Urban walking + wedding | Mix of casual + 2–3 dressier outfits; layers for evening |
| **Madrid** | Museums / parks | Comfortable daytime clothes; **Jun 4 Corpus Christi** — some shops closed, plan outfit night before |

### What NOT to over-pack

- Full suit/tux in checked luggage (Chandler rents locally)
- Heavy jeans for every day (one pair enough)
- More than one "nice" outfit per person outside wedding gear
- Bulky hair tools if using pro styling at hotel

### Carry-on essentials

- 1 change of clothes per person (lost luggage hedge)
- All medications, documents, chargers
- Wedding-adjacent items: bow tie backup
- Sagrada Família app downloaded + ticket locators saved offline

## Financial

- Notify banks of international travel
- Credit cards with no foreign transaction fees
- Plan for ATM cash withdrawals

## Apps to Download

- Trip Calendar (subscribe/download from site)
- Renfe (trains)
- Google Maps (download offline maps!)

# Valencia Decoded

*Your window: May 27–29, 2026. Beach house, paella, then the train north.*

---

## The 60-Second Orientation

Valencia is Spain's third-largest city (~800,000 in the municipality; ~1.6M in the metro) sitting on a flat coastal plain where the Turia River once ran straight through town before a 1957 flood killed dozens and forced the river into a bypass channel. What you get today is unusual: a major European city that still feels provincial, food-obsessed, and slightly overlooked compared with Barcelona and Madrid.

Politically, Valencia is the capital of the **Comunitat Valenciana** — an autonomous region with its own language (Valencià, a Catalan dialect by any linguistic measure, though local politicians will debate you on that), its own parliament in Alicante's shadow, and a regional government dominated since 2023 by the **Partido Popular (PP)**. Nationally, Valencians vote somewhat right of center; regionally, the PP runs the show. The city proper leans more mixed — Compromís (a left-green regionalist party) has held the mayor's office before and still shapes urban policy.

What makes Valencia strategically interesting: it is a **Mediterranean port + agricultural hinterland + emerging tech/tourism hub**, connected to Madrid by high-speed rail in under two hours. You arrive by AVE on your first night. That rail link is not convenience — it is the modern expression of a city that has always lived off movement of goods and people.

---

## Deep History: War, Conquest, and Turning Points

**Roman Valentia (138 BC).** Founded for retired soldiers — already a pattern of military colonization. The Romans laid out a grid; fragments survive under the old city.

**Visigoths, then Moors (714 AD).** Islamic Valencia became a prosperous taifa (mini-kingdom). The Moors built the irrigation system — *acequias* — that still waters the huerta (market garden belt) around the city. Orange groves you see from the train are not scenery; they are 1,000-year-old infrastructure.

**El Cid (1094).** Rodrigo Díaz captured Valencia from the Moors and ruled briefly — rare medieval case of a mercenary warlord holding a major city. His mythologized version dominates Spanish nationalism; the real story is messier (he served both Christian and Muslim paymasters).

**Reconquista (1238).** James I of Aragon took the city. Valencia joined the Crown of Aragon — same political universe as Barcelona. Gothic churches rose atop mosques; Mudéjar (Islamic-craftsmen-under-Christian-rule) architecture defines the old center.

**Golden Age (15th–16th centuries).** Valencia's silk trade and ceramics (azulejos) made it rich. The **Lonja de la Seda** (Silk Exchange, UNESCO) is the physical receipt — a secular cathedral of commerce. This is when paella's ancestors appear in the huerta: farmers' one-pan rice dishes, not tourist seafood.

**War of the Spanish Succession (1707).** Valencia backed the losing Habsburg claimant. Bourbon victory meant centralization from Madrid, suppression of regional fueros (charters). Sound familiar? Catalonia's 1714 trauma has a Valencian echo — less remembered, equally real.

**1800s–1930s.** Industrial port growth, orange export boom, early tourism. The city expanded beyond medieval walls.

**Spanish Civil War (1936–1939).** Valencia served as the **Republican capital** from November 1936 until the fall of Catalonia — the government sat here while Madrid fought on. Franco’s victory meant repression, Spanish-only policy, and decades of Madrid-centric investment. Bombs hit the city; memory was later buried.

**1957 flood.** A Mediterranean cut-off low (sound familiar?) drowned the old riverbed. The city diverted the Turia and turned the dry channel into **Jardines del Turia** — nine kilometers of park through the urban core. One of the great post-disaster urban reinventions in Europe.

**Democracy (1978 onward).** Autonomous status restored. Valencià language back in schools — contested ever since. Expo-like projects culminated in Calatrava's **City of Arts and Sciences** (1990s–2000s): love it or hate it, it rebranded a city that had been sleeping.

**DANA, October 2024.** A isolated high-altitude depression dropped a year's rain in hours on the southern metro area (Utiel, Paiporta, Sedaví — not your beach neighborhood, but the same region). **229+ dead.** The regional emergency response became a national scandal: delayed mobile alerts, political finger-pointing, massive street protests. Reconstruction and blame are still live politics when you visit.

---

## Architecture You Can Read

Walk the city as a timeline:

| What you see | Era | What it means |
|--------------|-----|---------------|
| **Torres de Serranos / Quart** | Gothic 14th c. | Medieval gate towers — defense when Valencia was a walled mercantile city |
| **La Lonja de la Seda** | Late Gothic 1480s | Merchant power — UNESCO for a reason; look at the spiral columns |
| **Mercado Central** | Modernisme 1914 | Iron, glass, tile — Valencia's answer to Les Halles; still a working market |
| **El Miguelete / Cathedral** | Mixed centuries | Roman foundations, Gothic bell tower you can climb |
| **Estació del Nord** | Modernisme 1917 | Your train to Barcelona departs from a ceramic-decorated jewel box |
| **Jardines del Turia** | 1970s–present | Flood bypass turned linear park — joggers, playgrounds, museums |
| **Ciutat de les Arts i les Ciències** | 1998–2005 | Calatrava's white whale — film sets, opera, Oceanogràfic aquarium |

Your beach house sits in **Poblats Marítims** — formerly independent fishing villages (Malvarrosa, Cabanyal) absorbed by the growing city. The port and beach promenade reflect 19th-century bourgeois summer culture, not ancient Rome.

**Military lens:** Valencia's flat terrain made it easy to defend with walls but nightmare to drain. Hydrology IS strategy here. The 1957 flood and 2024 DANA both hit the same lesson: Mediterranean flash floods are predictable in category, lethal in timing.

---

## Politics Now

**Spain (national).** Prime Minister **Pedro Sánchez** (PSOE) governs with a fragile coalition — Sumar on the left, plus parliamentary support from Catalan and Basque nationalist parties. His 2023 return required a **Catalan amnesty law** that sparked nationwide protests. In February 2026, Spain's Constitutional Court issued a complex ruling on that law — parts moot, constitutional questions still live. **Vox** (hard right) pressures the PP from the right. Next general election: due by **late 2027**.

**Comunitat Valenciana (regional).** **PP** controls the Generalitat. **Carlos Mazón** (president during the 2024 DANA) became the face of institutional failure — late civil alerts, absent leadership during critical hours, months of protests demanding resignation. The disaster is now a case study in **decentralized disaster management**: autonomous communities run civil protection until they ask Madrid for help — and voters decide if they waited too long.

**València city.** Mayor **María José Catalá** (PP) since 2023. Tensions with regional PP over flood accountability. Urban issues: **tourism saturation**, **housing costs** rising faster than wages, debate over port expansion and beachfront development (Cabanyal neighborhood was saved from demolition after years of fight).

**Language politics.** Valencià is co-official. You will see **dual signage** (Valencià/Castellano). Calling it "a dialect of Catalan" in the wrong bar starts an argument. Practical rule: locals switch freely; you should not force the issue.

---

## Demographics, Economy, and Cultural Shifts

**Numbers (Comunitat Valenciana, ~5.5M people in 2025–26):**
- Population **growing ~1.8% annually** — roughly double the Spanish average, driven by immigration
- **~20% foreign nationals**; **~24% born outside Spain**
- **Aging**: ~20% over 64 — retirement migration to the coast is real
- **Coastal concentration**: more than half the regional population lives in 60 coastal municipalities

**Economy:** Agriculture (citrus, vegetables, wine) still matters more than tourists assume. Port logistics, ceramics, furniture, and automotive supply chains. Tourism is huge but seasonally skewed — May is shoulder-to-high season warming up. Tech and events (see post-trip festivals) are deliberate diversification plays.

**Cultural shifts:**
- Valencia competes with Barcelona for **digital nomads and remote workers** — lower cost, beach, rail to Madrid
- **Housing protest politics** echo Barcelona: locals priced out of city center
- Post-DANA: **institutional trust crisis** — "they knew the flood risk and did nothing" is a common street sentiment in affected areas
- Food identity remains the strongest cultural glue — paella wars are semi-serious

---

## While You Are Here (May 27–29, 2026)

**No major festival blocks your dates.** You miss Las Fallas (March) and the massive summer events. What you get:

| Date | Context |
|------|---------|
| **Wed May 27** | Arrive ~22:00 after AVE. Check-in 16:00 window passed — late arrival. Host Maria Pilar needs your ETA. |
| **Thu May 28** | **Paella 13:00** at Casa Carmela. Full flexible day. **Clóchinas** (local mussels) in season. Sunset ~21:15. |
| **Fri May 29** | Leave ~07:45 for 09:06 train. Vrbo checkout nominally 11:00 — you are gone early. |

**Weather:** High 24–28°C, lows ~16°C. Mediterranean spring — bright, dry, UV real.

**After you leave:** Festival de Jazz (from Jun 24), BIGSOUND urban music (Jun 26–27), **Gay Games XII** (Jun 27–Jul 4) — Valencia will shift into major-event mode. Signage and hotel staffing may already be ramping by late May.

**Closures:** None expected for your dates except normal Sunday/holiday patterns (May 29 is Friday — full services).

**Note:** You arrive **four days after** a heavy news week (teacher strike marches May 23, Valencia–Barcelona match May 23). Effects may linger — school disruptions, residual traffic patterns, heightened political mood — but no event blocks your dates directly.

---

## Local News (Spring 2026)

*What Valencians were arguing about the week before you land — useful context for reading the room.*

**Indefinite teacher strike (since May 11).** Unions STEPV, UGT, CCOO, and CSIF called an **indefinite strike** across public schools and universities, demanding better staffing ratios, infrastructure fixes (elevators, A/C, accessibility), and pay. A **mass march on Saturday May 23** (18:00 from Plaça de Sant Agustí → Plaça de l'Ajuntament) drew families in pink shirts alongside teachers in green — the fifth major demo in two weeks. Education minister **Némesio Ortí** says she will keep negotiating; unions say talks are stalled. **For you:** if any family has school-age curiosity, public schools may still be disrupted late May. Unlikely to affect tourism; very likely to dominate local radio and TV.

**Turia park renovation — politics in the dry riverbed.** Mayor **María José Catalá** (PP) approved a **€16.5M rehab** of Turia trams X–XI (near Palau de la Música). Controversy: a **new pond under Pont de l'Àngel Custodi**, originally a Vox proposal to deter homeless encampments in the park. Catalá adopted a softened version; left-wing groups call it cruel architecture. **For you:** if you walk the Turia, you are seeing live urban-policy battleground — not just a park.

**Valencia CF vs Peter Lim (May 23).** Supporters group **Libertat VCF** marched May 23 (~17:00, Plaça de l'Ajuntament → Mestalla) before **Valencia–Barcelona** La Liga (14:00 kickoff). Fans accuse Singaporean owner **Peter Lim** of asset-stripping the club; mayor Catalá has never publicly responded to a 20,000-person 2024 protest, fueling rage. **For you:** match day traffic near Mestalla May 23; by May 27 the city has moved on — but bar talk about Lim is evergreen.

**DANA accountability — still the regional open wound.** October 2024 floods killed **229+**; regional president **Carlos Mazón** (PP) faces ongoing protests and judicial scrutiny over **delayed ES-Alert messages** and his whereabouts during critical hours. Reconstruction law (April 2025) fast-tracks rebuilding in affected municipalities. **For you:** do not bring up DANA lightly with strangers unless they do first; in affected southern districts it is grief + fury, not tourism small talk.

**Gearing up for summer mega-events.** Jazz Festival (from Jun 24), **BIGSOUND** (Jun 26–27 at Ciutat de les Arts), **Gay Games XII** (Jun 27–Jul 4) — hotel and venue prep may already be visible late May.

---

## Key Vocabulary

| Word / phrase | Language | Meaning | When you'll hear it |
|---------------|----------|---------|---------------------|
| **Paella** | Castellano | Rice dish — *Valenciana* = rabbit/chicken/beans; *marinera* = seafood | Every restaurant; locals have opinions |
| **Paella valenciana** | Castellano | The "real" paella (no seafood) | Casa Carmela — use this term |
| **Clóchinas** | Valencià / Castellano | Local mussels (in season May–Jun) | Markets, beach restaurants |
| **Horchata** | Castellano | Tiger-nut milk drink | Horchaterías; with *fartons* (pastry sticks) |
| **Huerta** | Castellano | Irrigated farmland belt around city | Explains oranges, paella rice origin |
| **Fallera / Fallas** | Valencià | Festival figures; Las Fallas = March fire festival | Context for city identity (you miss the event) |
| **Comunitat Valenciana** | Valencià | Autonomous region (3 provinces) | News, politics |
| **Generalitat Valenciana** | Valencià | Regional government | Strike negotiations |
| **DANA** | Acronym | *Depresión Aislada en Niveles Altos* — cut-off storm | 2024 disaster; still raw |
| **Senyera** | Valencià | Red/yellow striped flag (shared with Catalonia) | Balconies — regional identity |
| **Bon dia / Bona nit** | Valencià | Good morning / Good night | Friendly default |
| **Quina hora teniu?** | Valencià | What time do you have? (for check-in) | Message Maria Pilar |
| **El compte, si us plau** | Valencià | The check, please | Restaurants |
| **Estació del Nord** | Valencià | North Station (your May 29 train) | Not to be confused with Joaquín Sorolla (AVE) |
| **Poblats Marítims** | Valencià | Maritime villages (Malvarrosa, Cabanyal) | Your beach neighborhood |
| **Arroz al horno** | Castellano | Oven-baked rice — another local staple | Alternative to paella |
| **Agora / ara mateix** | Valencià | Now / right now | Urgency |
| **Manifestació** | Valencià | Protest march | May 23 news; may still echo |
| **Vaga indefinida** | Valencià | Indefinite strike | Teacher strike context |

**Tip:** Valencians often code-switch mid-sentence. Reply in **Castellano** unless someone opens in Valencià — both are welcome, forcing neither is the grace move.

---

## On the Ground

**Look for:**
- **Orange trees** on sidewalks — decorative now, but symbol of huerta wealth
- **Ceramic tile** on facades — azulejo tradition
- **Bilingual signs** — Valencià first on many official boards
- **Beach promenade culture** — families, cyclists, evening paseo
- **Flood markers / memorial graffiti** in city center referencing DANA — political, not tourist

**Listen for:**
- Valencià in markets and neighborhoods; Castellano everywhere in tourism
- Pride in **authentic paella** — seafood paella is tolerated, not revered

**Kid-friendly hook:**
- The old river is now a park — "they moved the river because it flooded the city"
- Romans, Moors, and knights all wanted this place because of the port and the garden

**Skip with kids:** DANA protest politics unless they ask — stick to "big rainstorm, city helping neighbors rebuild"

---

## Rabbit Holes

| Resource | Why |
|----------|-----|
| **Jason Webster, *Guerra* / *Duende*** | Accessible modern Spain with Valencian threads |
| **Paul Preston, *The Spanish Civil War*** | Valencia as Republican capital — context for 1930s |
| **Lonja de la Seda (visit)** | Best 30-minute architecture hit in the old city |
| **Documentary: 2024 DANA coverage** (El País, BBC) | Understand why flood politics still simmer |
| **Map: Jardines del Turia** | Walk one segment — urban planning as disaster response |

---

*Last updated: May 23, 2026. Politics and event dates verified against public sources; check day-of for strikes or weather alerts.*

# Barcelona Unpacked

*Your window: May 29–June 1, 2026. Wedding weekend, Gaudí, Gothic Quarter.*

---

## The 60-Second Orientation

Barcelona is the capital of **Catalonia** (Catalunya) — 1.6 million in the city, 5.7 million in the metro — and the most economically powerful region in Spain. It is also the place where many Spaniards feel least "Spanish." Catalans run their own schools (Catalan-first education), police (Mossos d'Esquadra), health system, and broadcast media. The independence referendum of **October 2017** failed legally, succeeded emotionally, and still defines the mood.

For you, Barcelona is wedding terrain: the **Gothic Quarter (Barri Gòtic)** is Roman, medieval, and tourist-saturated all at once. Your Eixample apartment sits on **Carrer de València** — not Valencia the city, but a grid street named after the city you just left. Welcome to Cerdà's 19th-century urban machine.

Barcelona makes money from **port, industry, tourism, and tech** — in that rough historical order. What changed everything visible: **1880s–1910s Modernisme** (Gaudí era), **1992 Olympics** (waterfront + global brand), and **2010s tourism explosion** (love/hate).

---

## Deep History: War, Conquest, and Turning Points

**Barcino (Roman colony).** Founded under Emperor Augustus. The Roman wall defines the Gothic Quarter's shape — you can still touch it in the MUHBA museum.

**Visigoths, then Moors (8th century).** Brief; Barcelona's story is really **Catalan + Mediterranean**, not Andalusian.

**County of Barcelona → Crown of Aragon (801–1469).** Barcelona became the maritime hub of an empire stretching to Naples, Sicily, Athens. Medieval wealth built the Gothic churches you walk past for the wedding. Catalán was a language of kings and merchants, not peasants.

**Union with Castile (1469).** Ferdinand of Aragon married Isabella of Castile — Spain as we know it. Barcelona's commercial elite lost primacy to Seville and later Madrid.

**1714 — The Siege.** War of Spanish Succession. Barcelona backed the Habsburgs. Bourbon victory on **11 September** (still Catalonia's national day — *Diada*) meant loss of institutions, banning of Catalan in administration, construction of the **Ciutadella fortress** to watch the conquered city. This date is tattooed on regional identity.

**Industrial 19th century.** Textiles, workers' movements, anarchism — Barcelona was the most radical city in Spain pre–Civil War.

**1888 / 1929 Expos.** Urban expansion, Montjuïc developed, Modernisme flourished.

**Spanish Civil War (1936–1939).** Barcelona was anarchist/republican heartland until Franco's conquest in January 1939. Bombings, purges, then **40 years of Franco**: Catalan banned in public life, street names Castilianized, FC Barcelona as covert national symbol.

**Democracy (1978 onward).** Autonomy restored. **1992 Olympics** — the beach you see did not exist as leisure space; it was industrial port. The Games rewrote the coastline and global image.

**2017 independence crisis.** Referendum, police violence, leaders jailed or exiled, amnesty law years later (2024). Movement is quieter now but **identity politics is ambient noise**, not a settled issue.

**Post-COVID tourism wars.** "Tourists go home" graffiti, limits on short-term rentals, water protests — Barcelona is actively managing its own success.

---

## Architecture You Can Read

| Layer | Where | What to notice |
|-------|-------|----------------|
| **Roman** | Barri Gòtic | Wall fragments, grid under medieval streets |
| **Gothic** | Cathedral, Santa Maria del Mar | Vertical stone — merchant wealth, not royal |
| **Modernisme** | Eixample, Passeig de Gràcia | Gaudí, Domènech i Montaner, Puig i Cadafalch — organic facades, trencadís mosaics |
| **Cerdà grid** | Eixample | 1859 octagonal blocks, chamfered corners — airflow and traffic before cars |
| **Olympic** | Port Olímpic, Montjuïc | 1992 pivot to sea |
| **Contemporary** | Glòries, 22@ district | Tech hub rebranding |

**Your wedding weekend hits:**
- **La Pedrera (Casa Milà)** — Gaudí apartment block; morning tour May 30
- **Sagrada Família** — still under construction after 140+ years; church as perpetual project
- **Gothic Quarter** — medieval street canyon; hard to photograph, easy to get lost (feature, not bug)

**Military lens:** After 1714, the Ciutadella was a **occupation fort in the city center** — demolished later, replaced by the park and zoo. Barcelona's urban form still reacts to conquest.

---

## Politics Now

**Catalonia (regional).** Governed by a shifting coalition — since 2024, **Salvador Illa** (PSC, Catalan wing of PSOE) as president after years of pro-independence majorities. Independence parties (ERC, Junts) still matter but lack 2017 momentum. **Language**: Catalan dominant in schools and official life; ~50%+ of metro population born outside Catalonia — integration friction is constant.

**Barcelona city.** Mayor **Jaume Collboni** (PSC) from 2024, replacing **Ada Colau** (Barcelona en Comú, left-green). Colau fought tourism and superblocks; Collboni signals **pragmatism** — keep economy humming, manage housing. Short-term rental crackdowns continue.

**Spain (national).** Sánchez needs Catalan party votes in Madrid's Congress — gives Catalonia leverage on amnesty, funding, infrastructure. **Amnesty law (2024)** and Constitutional Court review (2026) remain emotionally raw: for supporters, healing; for opponents, rule-of-law betrayal.

**Right wing.** PP + **Vox** coalition possible in future — Vox is especially strong where immigration and Catalan identity collide.

**Street level:** Senyera (Catalan flag) on balconies; **estelada** (starred independence flag) less common than 2017 but still visible; Spanish flags often deliberate counter-signal.

---

## Demographics, Economy, and Cultural Shifts

**Barcelona metro (~5.7M):**
- **~22% foreign-born** — Latin America, Morocco, Pakistan, Romania largest groups
- Low birth rate; growth from immigration
- **Tourism**: pre-COVID ~30M overnight stays/year — crushing for old city infrastructure
- **Unemployment** historically higher than Madrid; youth job quality a grievance

**Economy:** Port of Barcelona is Mediterranean top tier. Industry (chemicals, autos) in belt around city. **Tech/startups** in 22@ and Poblenou. Fashion, design, medical research. Wedding tourism is niche but yours is part of a bigger events economy.

**Shifts you'll feel:**
- **Housing crisis** — locals vs Airbnb (your VRBO is part of the debate)
- **Superblocks (superilles)** — pedestrian priority pilots; some love, some hate
- **Water stress** — Mediterranean drought politics; don't waste tap water loudly
- **Shift from independence to "liveability"** — younger Catalans often prioritize rent over flags

---

## While You Are Here (May 29–June 1, 2026)

| Date | What matters |
|------|----------------|
| **Fri May 29** | Train in ~12:20, check-in 14:00. **Welcome party 7 PM** — [Alaire Rooftop](https://tmg.link/app/r/condes). Suit fitting at Casa Gay if scheduled. |
| **Sat May 30** | **Tour day:** [La Pedrera 09:15](https://tmg.link/app/r/lapedrera), Sagrada 12:15 entry, [tapas 17:00 at Catedral](https://tmg.link/app/r/catedralbcn). |
| **Sun May 31** | **[Shuttle pickup 4:30 PM](https://tmg.link/app/r/shuttlepickup)**, ceremony & reception. ~77°F at ceremony, ~70°F by midnight. |
| **Mon Jun 1** | Checkout 11:00, train to Madrid 15:00. Suit return AM. |

**Primavera Sound** (major indie/rock festival) runs **June 3–7** at Parc del Fòrum — you leave **before** it starts, but **setup and crew** may already stress transit near Montjuïc/Sants by June 1. Allow buffer getting to Barcelona-Sants.

**Corpus Christi** is **June 4** — you will be in Madrid by then, but Barcelona's Catholic calendar may affect late-May church events and flower displays in some parishes.

**Weather:** 18–29°C (65–85°F) per Joe (May 24) — warm and sunny wedding weekend. ~25°C (77°F) at ceremony Sunday, ~21°C (70°F) by midnight.

**Crowds:** Late May = high tourism + wedding season. Gothic Quarter will be packed. Book nothing assuming walk-in.

**Note:** National **housing protests** hit Madrid May 24 (Atocha) — before you arrive. Barcelona overtourism policy fights are in headlines weekly. You land in a country mid-argument about who cities are *for*.

---

## Local News (Spring 2026)

**Collboni's war on tourist flats (your VRBO is in the crosshairs).** Mayor **Jaume Collboni** (PSC) pledged to **revoke all ~10,000 licensed tourist apartment permits by November 2028** — Europe's toughest anti-Airbnb move. Existing bookings remain legal; the fight is about whether Barcelona should keep hosting visitors like you or force units back to long-term rentals. Opposition says the city will lose **Primavera Sound**, MWC, and 40,000 jobs; Collboni says housing is existential. **April 2026:** general tourist tax increased again — hotels ~€10–17/night, vacation rentals ~€14/night. **For you:** your Eixample VRBO is legal now; understand locals may side-eye short-term guests. Do not debate Airbnb at the wedding bar unless invited.

**Cruise tax doubled — fast-tracked.** Collboni pushed to **double the overnight cruise passenger tax** from €4 to €8 immediately (not phased over four years). Goal: discourage day-tripping cruise crowds that swamp the Rambla without spending locally. Terminal count cut from seven to five. **For you:** minimal direct impact; explains anti-tourism graffiti.

**Primavera Sound (Jun 3–7) loading in.** One of Europe's biggest indie festivals sets up at **Parc del Fòrum** right after you leave Jun 1. By May 30–31 you may see freight, fencing, and extra transit near the waterfront. **200,000+** accommodation nights historically — city already in festival-season metabolism.

**Catalan amnesty law — Constitutional Court (Feb 2026).** Spain's TC issued a complex ruling on the **2024 amnesty** for 2017 independence process defendants — partial loss of object, constitutional questions alive. Catalonia watches whether reconciliation or betrayal wins. Street temperature: lower than 2017, but **identity is not settled**.

**Housing = national spring storyline.** Madrid march May 24; Barcelona's left (Comuns) wants **€50M diverted from tourism promotion to housing**. Slogan in streets: *"pisos per viure-hi, no per especular"* — homes to live in, not to speculate.

**Sagrada completion timeline.** Still no end date — church generates more tourism revenue unfinished than many finished cathedrals. Your May 30 entry is peak bucket-list season; expect security lines even with tickets.

---

## Key Vocabulary

| Word / phrase | Language | Meaning | When you'll hear it |
|---------------|----------|---------|---------------------|
| **Barcelona / Barna** | Castellano / slang | City name / local shorthand | Barna = insider casual |
| **Català** | Catalan | Catalan language | Street signs, schools, politics |
| **Castellano** | Castellano | Spanish (not "Spanish" to Catalans) | Default with visitors |
| **Senyera** | Catalan | Catalan flag (stripes) | Balconies |
| **Estelada** | Catalan | Independence flag (blue star) | Politics |
| **Barri Gòtic** | Catalan | Gothic Quarter | Wedding zone |
| **Eixample** | Catalan | 19th-century grid district | Your apartment |
| **Passeig de Gràcia** | Catalan | Gaudí avenue | La Pedrera tour meetup |
| **Modernisme** | Catalan | Art Nouveau movement | Architecture tours |
| **Trencadís** | Catalan | Broken-tile mosaic (Gaudí) | Sagrada, Park Güell |
| **Sagrada Família** | Catalan | "Holy Family" basilica | Tickets, tours |
| **Tapas / tapes** | Castellano / Catalan | Small plates | Evening tour |
| **Pa amb tomàquet** | Catalan | Bread rubbed with tomato + oil | Every meal starter |
| **Cava** | Catalan | Sparkling wine (not Champagne) | Toasts — say *cava*, not champagne |
| **Vermut** | Catalan | Vermouth hour (Sunday pre-lunch drink) | Bars ~12:00–14:00 |
| **Sopar** | Catalan | Dinner (late — 21:00+) | Wedding timing |
| **Mossos** | Catalan | Catalan police force | Autonomy symbol |
| **Generalitat** | Catalan | Catalan regional government | News |
| **Procés** | Catalan | "The process" — independence movement | 2017 era term |
| **Pis turístic** | Catalan | Tourist apartment | Housing politics |
| **Multitudinària** | Catalan | Massive (crowd) | News about demos |
| **Bon dia / Bona tarda** | Catalan | Good morning / afternoon | Greet in Catalan first in shops |
| **Quant és?** | Catalan | How much is it? | Markets |
| **L'addició, si us plau** | Catalan | The bill, please | Restaurants |
| **Gràcies / Merci** | Catalan | Thanks (formal / informal) | |

**Tip:** In Barcelona, a **"bon dia" in Catalan** before switching to English buys goodwill. Saying *"¿Hablas inglés?"* without trying Catalan first — fine in tourist core, eyeroll in Gràcia.

---

## On the Ground

**Flags:**
- **Senyera** (yellow/red stripes) — Catalan identity
- **Estelada** (blue star) — independence sympathy
- **Spanish flag** — often political statement on balconies

**Graffiti worth reading:**
- "Tourists go home" / "Flats for locals" — housing politics
- Independence slogans faded but not gone

**Sounds:**
- Catalan in neighborhoods; multilingual in tourist core
- **Castells** (human towers) — if you hear drums in a plaza, stop and watch

**Food timing:**
- Dinner culture starts **21:00+** — wedding schedules may already adapt for Americans

**With kids:**
- Gaudí buildings as "dragon houses"
- Gothic Quarter as "Narrow streets where knights walked"
- Beach at Barceloneta — crowded but fun; watch pickpockets

---

## Rabbit Holes

| Resource | Why |
|----------|-----|
| **Robert Hughes, *Barcelona*** | Best single-volume city biography |
| **MUHBA (History Museum)** | Roman Barcelona under your feet |
| **Palau de la Música Catalana** | Modernisme interior — even if you only peek |
| **Podcast: Catalonia geopolitics explainer** (BBC, NYT) | 2017 crisis primer |
| **1992 Olympics before/after photos** | Understand the beachfront |

---

*Last updated: May 23, 2026.*

# Madrid in Context

*Your window: June 1–4, 2026. Whole family Airbnb, tapas, departures — and Corpus Christi on your last day.*

---

## The 60-Second Orientation

Madrid is the **capital of Spain** and the **Comunidad de Madrid** region — ~3.3 million in the city, ~6.8 million in the metro. Unlike Barcelona or Valencia, it has **no Roman origin story and no port**. Philip II made it capital in **1561** because it was geographically central and politically neutral — a blank slate for imperial administration.

Today Madrid is where **money, government, media, and monarchy** concentrate. The king does not live in the big palace anymore, but the machinery of state surrounds you. Your Airbnb in **La Latina** puts you in pre-tourist Madrid — market streets, taverns, churches — ten minutes from **Puerta del Sol** (kilometer zero of Spain's road network) and **Plaza Mayor**.

Madrid runs **one hour behind Valencia/Barcelona** in political temperament: more Castilian, more national, less regionalist — but **Madrid region** has its own brand of conservative autonomy under **Isabel Díaz Ayuso** (PP), often at war with Sánchez's national government.

**Critical for your trip: Thursday June 4 is Corpus Christi — a public holiday.** Banks and many shops close. Thomas family flies out that afternoon; Williams checkout is 11:00. Plan food and cash accordingly.

---

## Deep History: War, Conquest, and Turning Points

**Pre-1561.** Small Moorish outpost (Mayrit = water channels). Castilian frontier town. No grand empire yet.

**1561 — Philip II moves the court.** Madrid becomes capital of the **Spanish Empire** at its zenith — silver from the Americas flows through Seville/Cádiz, decisions through Madrid. The **Palacio Real** (still Europe's largest royal palace by floor area) and monastic network expand.

**1700s — Bourbon Madrid.** Philip V and successors impose French-style urban planning — **Salón del Prado**, neoclassical ministries, rational boulevards.

**1808 — Dos de Mayo uprising.** Madrid rose against Napoleon's occupying forces — brutal reprisal, painted by Goya (*The Third of May 1808* in the Prado). Modern Spanish nationalism has a martyrdom date here too.

**Spanish Civil War (1936–1939).** Madrid **held out under siege** until the end — iconic republican resistance. Franco entered victorious; repression followed. Madrid swelled with rural migrants under Franco — castellanization, industrial belts, conservative Catholic culture.

**Democracy (1978 onward).** Explosive growth — **La Movida Madrileña** (late 70s–80s counterculture), EU membership, immigration boom, skyline rise in **AZCA / Cuatro Torres**.

**2004 Atocha bombings.** Islamist terrorist attack on commuter trains — 193 dead. National trauma; Atocha station (where your AVE arrives) is also a memorial site.

**2008 financial crisis.** Youth unemployment catastrophe; **Indignados (15-M) movement 2011** born in Madrid — precursor to global Occupy. Still shapes housing politics.

**COVID and after.** Tourism rebound; short-term rental fights; heat-island summers pushing 40°C by July (you miss the worst in early June).

---

## Architecture You Can Read

| Era | Examples | Story |
|-----|----------|-------|
| **Habsburg (Austrias)** | Plaza Mayor, Puerta del Sol area, San Isidro | 16th–17th c. imperial Madrid — austere brick |
| **Bourbon** | Palacio Real, Prado museum building, Retiro | Enlightenment scale — monarchy as theater |
| **19th c. expansion** | Gran Vía | Paris-style boulevard cut through medieval fabric |
| **Franco-era growth** | Peripheral barrios, social housing | Functional, dense |
| **Modern** | Cuatro Torres, AZCA | 21st-century finance skyline |

**Your neighborhood — La Latina / Tirso de Molina:**
- Medieval street pattern — narrow, sloping
- **Mercado de la Cebada / San Miguel** nearby (tourist tapas market)
- **Cava Baja / Cava Alta** — tavern streets where politicians still eat

**Retiro Park:** Once royal retreat, now democratic lung — rowboats, Crystal Palace, street performers.

**Military lens:** Madrid's centrality is **logistics** — radiating roads (Sol as hub), rail nodes (Atocha, Chamartín), air (Barajas). Empire was administered here; armies mustered through Castile. Civil War siege left psychological mark — "Madrid resiste" identity.

---

## Politics Now

**Spain (national).** Government in Madrid physically — Moncloa Palace, Cortes (Congress/Senate). **Sánchez** coalition fragile; opposition **PP + Vox** attacks on immigration, amnesty, energy policy. **2027 election** looms.

**Comunidad de Madrid (region).** **Isabel Díaz Ayuso (PP)** — high-profile, media-savvy, culture-warrior brand ("Madrid freedom" vs COVID lockdowns, low taxes narrative). Won landslides. Model for PP nationally. Clashes constantly with national left on health, housing, environment.

**Madrid city.** Mayor **José Luis Martínez-Almeida (PP)**. Cleaner than Ayuso rhetorically; same party. Focus on **events, tourism, mobility** — Madrid wants to be Barcelona's rival for conventions and nightlife.

**Monarchy.** King **Felipe VI** — low-key post-Juan Carlos scandals; monarchy accepted but not universally loved. Republican sentiment exists, quieter than Catalan independence.

**Street politics:** Housing protests (banners for rent control), taxi vs Uber fights, immigrant-rights marches — Madrid is where national debates hit pavement.

---

## Demographics, Economy, and Cultural Shifts

**Metro ~6.8M:**
- **~17% foreign-born** — Latin America largest share (Colombia, Venezuela, Peru), plus Moroccan, Romanian communities
- **Aging slower than rural Spain** — immigration keeps workforce young
- **Internal migration** from all regions — Madrid is Spain's melting pot

**Economy:** Finance, telecom, government, tourism, universities, healthcare. **No port** — Madrid sells services and power. Higher GDP per capita than national average. **Unemployment** improved post-COVID but youth still precarious.

**Cultural shifts:**
- **Late-night economy** — dinner 22:00, bars midnight, norm not exception
- **Secularization** — church attendance low except holidays (Corpus Christi still matters institutionally)
- **Football** — Real Madrid as global brand; Atlético as local grit identity
- **Rent crisis** — La Latina gentrifying; your short stay is in a desirable zone

---

## While You Are Here (June 1–4, 2026)

| Date | Plan impact |
|------|-------------|
| **Mon Jun 1** | AVE arrives **18:17** Atocha; Airbnb ~19:00. Earliest check-in 15:00 — no conflict. Light evening — jet lag + wedding recovery. |
| **Tue Jun 2** | Full explore day. Retiro, Prado if energy, tapas in La Latina. |
| **Wed Jun 3** | **Thomas family departs** DL0063 **14:45** Barajas — taxi ~12:00–12:30. Williams still in Madrid. |
| **Thu Jun 4** | **CORPUS CHRISTI — public holiday.** Checkout 11:00. **Williams JetBlue 2260 departs 14:05** — taxi ~12:00. Many shops/banks **closed**. Eat lunch early; confirm taxi night before. |

**Corpus Christi detail:**
- Major Catholic feast — **processions** possible near cathedral and center
- Madrid and Castile-La Mancha regions observe holiday closures
- **Mercado de San Miguel** may have reduced hours — have backup tapas spot in La Latina
- Not a party festival — solemn + family day; crowds near churches, not clubs

**Weather:** 28–32°C possible by June 4 — warm. Hydrate. Siesta is real.

**Events you miss (after you leave):**
- **Madrid Pride** (late June)
- **San Isidro** (May 15) — already passed
- **Veranos de la Villa** summer concerts

**Note:** You miss the **May 24 housing mega-march** (Atocha → Sevilla) by a week — but the grievances will still be on every terrace conversation.

---

## Local News (Spring 2026)

**"La vivienda nos cuesta la vida" — housing spring (May 24).** Dozens of groups including **Sindicato de Inquilinas** marched **Sunday May 24, 12:00 from Atocha** along Paseo del Prado → Alcalá → Metro Sevilla. Organizers claim rents up **50%+** in a decade; demand rent controls, end to abusive contracts, more public housing. Part of a **national "hot spring"** of housing demos (Guadalajara May 23, Madrid May 24, more to follow). **For you:** you arrive Jun 1 — protests done, but **posters, banners, and bitterness remain**. Your La Latina Airbnb sits in a neighborhood locals fear is pricing them out.

**Ayuso vs Metro Line 7B victims (May 22 ruling).** **El País** reported a court ordered **Comunidad de Madrid** to pay **€89,608 more** than offered to a couple whose home was demolished for **Metro Line 7B** construction in San Fernando de Henares — subsidence destroyed 73 buildings. President **Isabel Díaz Ayuso** had called earlier payouts "maximum legal." ~30 more families expect similar rulings — **million-euro liability** for regional government. **For you:** emblematic of Ayuso's "low taxes, fast growth" model colliding with courts; explains why she fights national housing regulation.

**New Madrid housing law (effective June 2026).** Regional government approved accelerated **social housing construction** — minister **Jorge Rodrigo**: *"build housing, build housing, and build housing."* Critics say it ignores rent caps; supporters say supply is the only fix. Debate mirrors national PP vs PSOE split you will feel in bar conversations.

**Corpus Christi (Jun 4 — YOUR checkout day).** Public holiday in Madrid and Castile. **Religious processions** near Almudena Cathedral and center; many **shops and banks closed**. Not a festival atmosphere — solemn, family, church-centric. **Mercado de San Miguel** may run reduced hours. **Plan:** stock breakfast night before; confirm taxi Jun 3; eat lunch early Jun 4 before airport.

**National context landing on Madrid:** Sánchez coalition survival, amnesty law court fight, **2027 election** positioning — Madrid media (El País, El Mundo, OK Diario) is the megaphone for all of it. Walk past **Moncloa** or **Congreso** and you are near the fault lines.

**Heat watch:** Early June can hit **30°C+**; 2026 spring has been warm. Retiro has shade; plan museum mornings.

---

## Key Vocabulary

| Word / phrase | Language | Meaning | When you'll hear it |
|---------------|----------|---------|---------------------|
| **Madrid** | Castellano | Capital city | |
| **La Latina** | Castellano | Your neighborhood (medieval + tapas) | Directions |
| **Sol** | Castellano | Puerta del Sol — "kilometer zero" | Tourist hub |
| **Casa** | Castellano | House / home — also "the firm" in business | *Vivienda* = housing as policy |
| **Vivienda** | Castellano | Housing (political word of 2026) | Protests, news |
| **Alquiler** | Castellano | Rent | Housing crisis core term |
| **Desahucio** | Castellano | Eviction | Protest slogans |
| **Tapas** | Castellano | Small plates (Madrid: often free with drink) | La Latina, Cava Baja |
| **Caña** | Castellano | Small beer | Order at bar |
| **Tinto de verano** | Castellano | Red wine + lemon soda — summer drink | Terrazas |
| **Terraza** | Castellano | Outdoor café seating | Full at 22:00 |
| **La hora de vermut** | Castellano | Vermouth o'clock (~noon Sunday) | Weekend tradition |
| **Comunidad de Madrid** | Castellano | Madrid region (not just city) | Ayuso's domain |
| **Ayuso** | Name | Regional PP president — polarizing | Politics |
| **Almeida** | Name | City mayor (PP) | Less flashy than Ayuso |
| **Madrid central** | Castellano | Low-emission zone downtown | Driving |
| **Atocha** | Castellano | Main train station — you arrive here | Jun 1 AVE |
| **Barajas** | Castellano | Airport (official name Adolfo Suárez) | Departures |
| **Corpus Christi** | Latin / Castellano | Jun 4 holiday — Body of Christ | Closures |
| **Procesión** | Castellano | Religious procession | Jun 4 streets |
| **Cerrado por festivo** | Castellano | "Closed for holiday" | Jun 4 signs |
| **El oso y el madroño** | Castellano | Bear and strawberry tree — city symbol | Sol statue |
| **Retiro** | Castellano | Main park | Jun 2 visit |
| **Prado / Reina Sofía** | Castellano | Art museums | Guernica at Reina Sofía |
| **Buenas / Qué tal** | Castellano | Hi / What's up | Casual greeting |
| **¿Me pones…?** | Castellano | "Can I get…?" (bar order) | Tapas bars |
| **La cuenta** | Castellano | The check | |
| **Hasta luego** | Castellano | See you later | |

**Tip:** Madrid Spanish is fast and direct — **"vale"** (okay) and **"venga"** (come on / let's go) are punctuation words. **"Madrid se cae"** (Madrid is falling apart) = hyperbolic local complaint about growth; not literal.

---

## On the Ground

**Notice:**
- **Kilometer zero plaque** at Puerta del Sol — all Spanish road distances start here
- **Bear and strawberry tree statue** — Madrid symbol (not a real bear eating a strawberry tree — it's a madroño)
- **Neoclassical uniformity** vs Barcelona's chaos — Madrid wants to look like a capital
- **Terrazas** full at 22:00 — locals, not tourists only
- **Police presence** near government buildings — normal

**With kids:**
- Retiro rowboats and Crystal Palace
- **Sobrino de Botín** (oldest restaurant claim) — story food
- Churros at **San Ginés** — late-night tradition you can do at 17:00 too

**Security:** Pickpockets in Sol, Gran Vía, metro — standard big-city rules

---

## Rabbit Holes

| Resource | Why |
|----------|-----|
| **Geoffrey Parker, *The Grand Strategy of Philip II*** | Why Madrid became capital of a global empire |
| **Goya in the Prado** | War, madness, modernity — 2-hour highlight reel |
| **Paul Preston on Civil War Madrid** | Siege mentality explained |
| **Walk: Los Austrias → La Latina → Lavapiés** | Three Madrids in one afternoon |
| **Podcast: 2004 Atocha** | Recent history at the station you arrive through |

---

*Last updated: May 23, 2026. **June 4 Corpus Christi** — treat as fixed constraint for departure day.*
